design_detail: Position paper of the National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME) Expert Panel on Evaluating and Reporting Opioid and Other Drug Deaths, published as a Review Article in the American Journal of Forensic Medicine and Pathology (received 4 March, accepted 7 March 2020). It updates the 2014 NAME and American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) position paper on opioid deaths, which had sunset under NAME policy; the CDC financially supported the earlier panel and supported this update. It answers six questions: which deaths need jurisdiction and autopsy; what scene investigation is needed; when to perform toxicology; how to collect specimens and what to test for; how post-mortem concentrations bear on certification; and how to certify cause, manner, how and where the injury occurred. No search, selection criteria, appraisal or grading of evidence is described; 53 references. Who wrote it (p. 152): 16 named authors and panel members (9 MD, 5 PhD, 2 BS), from pathology departments (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Washington, Wake Forest School of Medicine), medical examiner offices (Jefferson County, Alabama, for the first author; Cuyahoga, Broward, Hennepin, Dane and Clackamas counties; the Armed Forces Medical Examiner System), two coroner's offices (Boulder County, Colorado; Montgomery County, Ohio), forensic toxicology or laboratory organizations (Department of Forensic Genetics and Forensic Toxicology, National Board of Forensic Medicine, Sweden; NMS Labs; RTI International's Laboratory Quality Assurance and Proficiency Program), emergency medicine and medical toxicology (Rutgers New Jersey Medical School) and the American Medical Association's science and drug policy unit. Filed as a narrative review with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for position papers of professional bodies.
can_establish: What the NAME expert panel recommended in 2020 for investigating, testing, interpreting and certifying suspected drug deaths in the United States, and the reasons and citations it gave, citable as the panel's position.
cannot_establish: How accurate certification is with or without autopsy, toxicology or these practices, how often deaths are wrongly put down to drugs or missed, or whether following the recommendations improves the counts: no data are analysed, no evidence is graded, and the paper's claim that its 2014 predecessor improved certificate specificity rests on a before–after trend.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (position paper). NAME convened the panel with the CDC's support to review the 2014 paper, the literature published since, and the changing nature of drug deaths (p. 152, Introduction 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or selection criteria; the 53 references were chosen by the panel. The panel followed the same process as the 2014 panel (NAME position-paper guidelines, reference 3), which this paper does not describe.
sample.selection_effects: Practitioners of death investigation and toxicology, plus emergency medicine and medical toxicology and one AMA staff member; no member is listed from a vital-statistics agency or public health surveillance programme, and none as representing people who use drugs (five people are thanked for technical support, without affiliations, p. 158). The cited evidence on autopsy accuracy comes largely from general autopsy-discrepancy studies, some decades old.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The paper's guidance on who decides: the medical examiner or coroner assumes jurisdiction and determines cause and manner; consultation with a forensic pathologist or toxicologist is advised for difficult interpretation (p. 156, Cause of death 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Guidance when several drugs are found: list by generic name every drug judged to have caused or contributed to death, at concentrations sufficient to do so; do not list drugs judged to have played no role; in an example with eight substances detected (alprazolam, 6-acetylmorphine, morphine, codeine, hydrocodone, ethanol, acetaminophen, diphenhydramine) the parent drug heroin is certified rather than its metabolites (pp. 156–157, Cause of death 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Evidence cited for the main recommendations: autopsy-discrepancy and external-examination studies (references 6, 8–15), post-mortem CT studies (16–19), toxicology screening (29–31), specimen handling (23, 35–37), interpretation of concentrations (38–47) and certification guidance from NCHS and CDC (49, 52).
outcomes.operationalization: The panel's working definitions: autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause of death, except delayed deaths after hospital admission; toxicology for every decedent meeting any of eight circumstances; a drug is listed when present at a concentration sufficient to have caused or contributed to death in the circumstances; manner 'accident' for misuse without apparent intent of self-harm.

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis. Figures quoted from cited sources: certificate specificity for drugs causing overdose deaths rose from 75% (2012) to 88% (2017) (reference 2, p. 152); overdose deaths 47,055 in 2014 and 70,237 in 2017, with provisional 2018 data 4% below 2017 and 44% above 2014 (references 4 and 5, p. 152); diagnoses in error compared with autopsy in up to 20% to 30% of cases (references 6 and 8–13, p. 153); routine post-mortem CT in an Australian office cut its autopsy rate from 62% to 47% (reference 18, p. 153); in heroin and methadone deaths, the triad of cerebral oedema, pulmonary oedema and bladder distension on CT was 100% specific but 26% sensitive for opioid intoxication (reference 19, p. 153); NAME's standard of at most 250 autopsies per pathologist per year (reference 7, p. 153).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Position paper; the panel's process (NAME position-paper guidelines) is referenced but not described.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence is cited for some recommendations and not others; the 20% to 30% error range is supported by general autopsy studies and by a mortality data brief, not by studies of suspected overdose deaths; no study is cited on how accurate the circumstantial rules for attributing deaths to depressants or stimulants are.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A practitioners' consensus: autopsy for suspected overdose deaths (with post-mortem CT judged experimental), comprehensive toxicology with blood from the iliofemoral vein preferred and urine and vitreous retained, generic drug names on certificates and amendment once toxicology is interpreted, 'accident' as the usual manner, and caution in reading post-mortem concentrations. The evidence behind it is cited, not appraised.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and introduction call the recommendations evidence-based and “the best evidence-based practices at this time” (p. 152), but no search, appraisal or grading is described, and several recommendations rest on experience (protection of responders, p. 154) or on circumstantial rules (p. 156). The introduction says the 2014 paper accomplished its goal, shown by specificity rising from 75% to 88% after its publication (p. 152): a before–after trend with no comparison. The 20% to 30% error range (p. 153) comes from general autopsy-discrepancy studies (from 1912, 1979, 1980, 1987, 1993 and 2003) and a mortality data brief, not from suspected overdose deaths. The Summary's statement that using the recommendations will improve detection and reporting of opioid-related deaths (p. 157) is a prediction.

timeline.event: First NAME and ACMT panel, supported by the CDC; its paper appeared in Academic Forensic Pathology (2013) and was republished in the Journal of Medical Toxicology (2014) (reference 1, p. 152).
SAMHSA consensus panel's uniform standards and case definitions for opioid-related deaths (not cited by this paper; card sc_goldberger_2013).
Warner and Hedegaard: specificity of drugs on overdose death certificates rose from 75% in 2012 to 88% in 2017 (reference 2, as cited, p. 152).
NCHS reference guide for completing death certificates for drug toxicity deaths (reference 52).

Hancock et al. cite this paper as current NAME best practice and find, at one North Carolina centre, 265 of 2,719 suspected drug deaths (9.75%) with a non-drug final cause after full autopsy, some of them with negative toxicology (card sc_hancock_2024, this reader).
Smiley-McDonald et al.: in the 2018 census, 11.2% of US offices reported no access to toxicology, and 14.1% were NAME-accredited (card sc_smiley_mcdonald_2025, this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: The professional standard cited by later studies on the project's list (Hancock et al., 2024; Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). Its central recommendation, autopsy for every suspected overdose death, is argued from general autopsy-discrepancy studies and the absence of evidence that external examination is as accurate; the first study on the list to count the question in drug deaths (Hancock et al., 2024) gives an upper bound of about 10% of suspected drug deaths with another cause. The census data show that many offices lack the resources the paper assumes.

funding.funder: No separate funding statement. The text says the CDC provided financial support for the 2013 panel to meet, and that NAME convened this panel with the CDC's support (p. 152).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (p. 152, first-page footnote).
funding.affiliations_note: Two panel members are at laboratory organizations (NMS Labs, Horsham, Pennsylvania; RTI International's Laboratory Quality Assurance and Proficiency Program), and the paper recommends comprehensive toxicology for broad groups of deaths. The first author is an author of three cited works (references 1, 29 and 46). A panel member, Jerri L. McLemore (Department of Pathology, Wake Forest School of Medicine), has the same name and institution as the second author of Hancock et al. (2024). Acknowledged for technical support: Bruce A. Goldberger, Nicole Jones, Margaret Warner, Julie K. O'Donnell and Denise McNally (p. 158). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A multi-office study of suspected overdose deaths in which a certifier records a cause of death from investigation, external examination, toxicology and, where available, post-mortem CT before the autopsy, without seeing its findings, against an independent panel's cause after full autopsy; and an evaluation, against comparison jurisdictions, of whether adopting these recommendations changes the specificity and accuracy of drug-death counts.

domains.note: No search, dates or selection criteria; the panel chose the 53 references, and its process is only referenced (NAME guidelines), not described.
No appraisal or grading; the 20% to 30% error range cites general autopsy-discrepancy studies and a mortality data brief; the circumstantial attribution rules cite one source each.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 53 references include the first author (the 2014 paper and two studies); the main arguments rest on others' work.

Recommendations are not marked as resting on evidence or on judgment; the effect of the 2014 paper is asserted from a trend; responder-safety advice rests on ACMT members' experience; the Summary predicts improvement. Uncertainties are acknowledged elsewhere (no simple way to tell lethal from sublethal concentrations; redistribution unpredictable; tolerance unmeasurable; post-mortem CT experimental).

domains.domain: Balance of attention to deaths wrongly put down to drugs and drug deaths missed
domains.note: Both directions appear: autopsy to find other causes, warnings that a concentration in a published lethal range does not by itself make a drug the cause and that drugs that played no role should not be listed. But the practical rules lean toward attribution when drugs are present (depressants with drowsiness or snoring; stimulants with agitation or sudden collapse; analogues presumed to act like their parents), with no guidance on recording uncertainty about a drug's contribution and no data on how often either error occurs. Wrong attribution to drugs is the under-represented side.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a position paper; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, as the round brief directs, and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domains (search and appraisal, both high). The paper can be cited, attributed to the NAME expert panel, for its recommendations: autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause (except delayed deaths after hospital admission); toxicology for decedents meeting any of eight circumstances; retention of blood, urine and vitreous, with iliofemoral blood preferred and the sampling site labelled; a comprehensive panel reviewed periodically; listing by generic name every drug judged to have caused or contributed, avoiding 'mixed drug intoxication'; amending certificates once toxicology is interpreted; 'accident' for misuse without apparent intent of self-harm; and for its statements of the limits of post-mortem levels (lethal ranges, redistribution, tolerance, dose cannot be back-calculated). It cannot be cited for any error rate, for the effect of the 2014 paper, for the accuracy of its circumstantial attribution rules, or for the safety advice to responders as an established finding.

key_findings.finding: The six recommendations: (1) autopsy gives the best information for interpreting toxicology, circumstances, history and scene, and the panel considers it essential in apparent overdose deaths; (2) scene investigation includes reconciling prescriptions and medication counts and noting paraphernalia or other evidence of intoxicating substances; (3) retain blood, urine and vitreous humour whenever available, with iliofemoral blood preferred to more central sites; (4) a comprehensive toxicology panel including potent depressants, stimulants and antidepressants, with special testing for novel substances present in the community; (5) when death is attributed to a drug or drugs, as cause or contributing factor, list them by generic name in the autopsy report and death certificate; (6) the best manner for an overdose without any apparent intent of self-harm is 'accident'.

History: NAME and ACMT published a joint position paper on opioid deaths in 2014, after a CDC-supported panel of pathologists and toxicologists worked through 2013; that paper sunset under NAME policy, and NAME, with the CDC's support, convened a new panel that followed the same process and answered six questions.

The panel states that the 2014 paper accomplished its goal, shown by certificate specificity for drugs causing overdose deaths rising from 75% in 2012 to 88% in 2017, an improvement that led the CDC to support the update.
key_findings.note: A before–after trend with no comparison; the paper presents no evidence that the 2014 paper caused the change.

key_findings.finding: The panel recommends that a medical examiner or coroner assume jurisdiction and perform, or cause to be performed, an autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause of death; it states that no peer-reviewed article has shown external examination with strong evidence of illicit drug use to be as accurate as autopsy, and that diagnoses are in error, compared with autopsy, in up to 20% to 30% of cases.
key_findings.locator: Question 1 (which deaths require jurisdiction and autopsy), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 20% to 30% range cites references 6 and 8–13: general autopsy-discrepancy studies and a mortality data brief, not studies of suspected overdose deaths.

key_findings.finding: Post-mortem CT: routine CT as part of preliminary case evaluation in an Australian office cut its autopsy rate from 62% to 47%; in heroin and methadone deaths, cerebral oedema, pulmonary oedema and bladder distension together were 100% specific but only 26% sensitive for opioid intoxication; given few studies, the panel considers post-mortem CT experimental and not ready for routine use in suspected overdose deaths.

Workload: NAME's standard allows at most 250 autopsies per pathologist per year; the panel strongly recommends that offices receive enough funding and staff to autopsy suspected overdose deaths within that standard. NAME's standards allow autopsy to be deferred in delayed deaths after overdose (hospital admission before death), with review of the medical record and any admission blood or urine.

Toxicology: history, investigation and autopsy together are an insensitive indicator of drug intoxication; urine screening kits give incomplete evidence, are subject to false positives and are inadequate for establishing a cause of death. The panel recommends toxicology to identify and quantify controlled and illicit substances, and relevant novel drugs, in all decedents with any of: known history of prescription or illicit drug use; evidence of drug use at the scene; autopsy findings suggesting drug use; massive lung oedema and froth with no other explanation; suspected drug smuggling; no unequivocal cause at autopsy; a potential natural cause where a drug may also have contributed; or traumatic deaths.
key_findings.locator: Question 3 (when to perform toxicology), 1st paragraph and list items 1–8

key_findings.finding: Specimens: delay to autopsy, sampling technique and preservation contribute more to inaccuracy than the testing procedures; blood, urine and vitreous should be collected whenever available, with bile and gastric contents also relevant; because of post-mortem redistribution the iliofemoral vein is the best blood source, followed by subclavian, heart or aorta, or any intact vessel, with blood from a body cavity a last resort; each specimen is labelled with its anatomical source and kept at 4°C, blood in fluoride-oxalate (grey-top) tubes.
key_findings.locator: Question 4 (specimen collection and scope), 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Scope: an adequate opioid panel includes buprenorphine (norbuprenorphine), codeine, fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, loperamide, methadone, 6-acetylmorphine, morphine, oxycodone, oxymorphone, tapentadol and tramadol; a full panel adds benzodiazepines, antidepressants, muscle relaxants, sleep aids, ethanol, pain-adjunct medicines, stimulants and prevalent new psychoactive drugs; offices should review the panel's scope periodically.

Interpreting post-mortem concentrations: they must be read with the circumstances, history, scene and autopsy; published tables of toxicology results are often based on a few cases with little context; a drug can cause death below a reported lethal range, and a concentration within it does not necessarily make the drug the cause; post-mortem concentrations should not be used to calculate the amount taken; redistribution is unpredictable in size and direction and may not occur in every case, but should not be an excuse to avoid deciding; tolerance accounts for part of the overlap between therapeutic and lethal concentrations, and there is no reliable quantitative measure of tolerance before or after death.
key_findings.locator: Question 5 (interpretation of post-mortem concentrations), 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Heroin: the panel treats 6-acetylmorphine in a sample as “sufficient evidence to ascribe intoxication to heroin”; without it, a blood morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 may be considered evidence of heroin use, especially with paraphernalia at the scene. Solid-tissue concentrations are often uninterpretable beyond showing exposure.

Certification wording: complete the certificate with the most specific details available and amend it when toxicology results are known and interpreted (filing is sometimes required before they are); list the generic names of all drugs judged to have caused or contributed; avoid 'mixed drug intoxication' or 'polypharmacy' without naming drugs; list the parent drug rather than metabolites; the order of drugs matters little; do not record drugs that played no role, and do not list every detected substance under other significant conditions.
key_findings.locator: Question 6, 1st paragraph (p. 156); Cause of death, 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs (pp. 156–157); Other significant conditions (p. 157)

key_findings.finding: Circumstantial rules for attributing a role: if the decedent seemed drowsy, hard to wake or snored loudly, any central nervous system depressants present were likely to have played a role; if the decedent seemed unusually frantic, complained of burning up, or entered a frenzied state with unusual strength, any stimulants present were likely to have played a role and should be listed as causing death; contraction band necrosis also suggests a stimulant role; cocaine, amphetamines and methadone should be considered as causes when present and the history is of sudden collapse; structurally similar new compounds may be presumed to act like their better-studied parents.
key_findings.note: Each rule cites a single source (references 20, 50, 22, 51); no study of their accuracy is cited.

key_findings.finding: Manner of death: suicide requires indication of intent of self-harm, and taking opioids in excess for self-treatment or for their effects is not by itself suicide; assigning 'undetermined' routinely does not serve public health; deaths from misuse of opioids without apparent intent of self-harm should be classed 'accident', with 'undetermined' reserved for rare cases with evidence for more than one manner; 'homicide' should be reserved for intentional exposure to sedate or kill a specific person, not used to help a legal case.

How and where injury occurred: health departments hope for the decedent's relevant medical history, route of administration, source of the drug and formulation (Table 2), without personal identifiers; when the place of use is unknown, the place where the person became unresponsive or was found dead is entered.
key_findings.locator: How injury occurred; Where injury occurred; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Scene safety: the panel says fear that responders could be overcome by touching or inhaling potent opioids such as carfentanil has proved more theoretical than practical, citing ACMT members' emergency experience; nitrile gloves and N95 respirators are described as sufficient protection.
key_findings.note: Experience-based, not a study finding; ACMT's own position statement is cited (reference 27).

key_findings.finding: The panel says its recommendations are based on the best evidence in the medical literature at the time of review and that using them will improve the detection and reporting of opioid-related deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The 20% to 30% error range for diagnoses made without autopsy is supported by references 6 and 8–13, of which reference 8 is an NCHS data brief on overdose death counts and references 9–11 are general clinical autopsy-discrepancy studies (1912, 1979, 1993).
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be cited as an error rate for drug deaths certified without autopsy.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper presents the rise in certificate specificity from 75% (2012) to 88% (2017) as showing that the 2014 paper accomplished its goal.
reporting_issues.consequence: A causal claim from an uncontrolled trend; the rise cannot be attributed to the paper from this evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The recommendations are described as evidence-based throughout, but no method (search, selection, appraisal, grading, consensus procedure or external review) is described; the panel refers to itself as the 2019 position paper panel (p. 154) in a paper received on 4 March and accepted on 7 March 2020 (p. 152).
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of each recommendation cannot be judged from the paper; they should be cited as the panel's judgment.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction says the joint NAME and ACMT paper was published in 2014, while reference 1 gives Academic Forensic Pathology 2013 with a 2014 republication in the Journal of Medical Toxicology.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the earlier paper exists in two versions.
